title: Vestments and the garments of the Kingdom
subtitle: Nothing the priest wears is his own, and the prayers he says while putting it on say exactly that.
summary: The clergy do not dress for the Liturgy, they are vested, and every garment carries a name, a scriptural root, and a prayer said over it. From the holy apparel commanded in Exodus 28 and the Spirit-given craft of Exodus 31, through Clement of Rome, Polycrates of Ephesus, the Apostolic Constitutions and the canons of Laodicea and Trullo, to the sticharion, epitrachelion, zone, epimanikia, epigonation and phelonion of the Divine Liturgy as they are actually prayed.
origin: Discord, liturgics-forum: In the Likeness of Angels.

essay.text: Most people meet the vestments long before anyone explains them. You are standing somewhere near the back. The doors in the icon screen open and a man comes out in a wide sleeveless garment with a long strip of embroidered cloth hanging from his neck, stiff cuffs laced at his wrists, a belt. Another man beside him lifts a narrow band of cloth into the air with two fingers every time he sings a petition. Three weeks later everything is red, then dark, then white. Nobody says why, because everyone around you has known since childhood. The easy conclusion is that this is decoration, or costume, and that it is not for you. That is a real loss, because the vestments are one of the plainest teaching instruments the Church owns. Every piece has a name, a scriptural root, and a short prayer said over it in a low voice while it goes on. This study is that explanation, worked from Aaron forward.
The command comes before the beauty

The first thing Scripture says about liturgical clothing is that God ordered it. "And thou shalt make holy apparel for Aaron thy brother, for honour and glory" (Exodus 28:2, in the Septuagint text this app serves). The materials are listed: gold, blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen. So are the garments: the breast-plate, the shoulder-piece, the full-length robe, the fringed tunic, the tire, the girdle. Three chapters later the craftsman is named, Beseleel, and God says of him, "I have filled him with a divine spirit of wisdom, and understanding, and knowledge, to invent in every work" (Exodus 31:3). Notice what that does. The skill to make a beautiful thing for the sanctuary is itself called a gift of the Spirit, not a worldly concession the sanctuary has to tolerate. Ezekiel supplies the other half of the rule. The priests put on linen inside the inner court, and when they go out to the people "they shall put off their robes, in which they minister, and they shall lay them up in the chambers of the sanctuary" (Ezekiel 44:19). The garments are not the man's wardrobe. They belong to the service, and they stay in it. As for the colours, Scripture names the dyes without assigning a meaning to each one verse by verse. The familiar readings, gold for glory, blue for the heavenly commandments, purple for kingship, scarlet for blood, are the Church's later reflection on them, and the yearly cycle of vestment colours differs between local traditions rather than being fixed by any canon.
The Church inherited the pattern, she did not invent it

A common objection is that all of this is Byzantine embroidery laid over a simple apostolic meal. The documents do not support that. Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth at the end of the first century, already reasons from the Aaronic orders: the high priest, the priests, the Levites and the layman each have their own place and their own ministrations. Around 190 Polycrates of Ephesus writes to Rome that the Apostle John, "being a priest, wore the sacerdotal plate", the golden petalon of Exodus 28 engraved with "Holiness of the Lord". The fourth-century Apostolic Constitutions simply direct the bishop, immediately before the anaphora, to "put on his shining garment" and stand at the altar, and offer no explanation at all, which is how people write about things everyone already knows. In the same century the Council of Laodicea has to forbid subdeacons, readers and singers to wear an orarion, and a vestment does not get forbidden to the lower orders unless it already marks a higher one. Three centuries after that the Council in Trullo is still legislating what clergy may wear in the street. Jerome thought the subject large enough to spend a whole letter on it, Letter 64 to Fabiola, a mystical exposition of the high priest's garments. What developed over the centuries was the cut and the ornament. The principle was there from the beginning.
What the priest actually says while he puts it on

The vesting is not silent. In the Byzantine rite the deacon first carries his sticharion and orarion to the priest and asks him to bless them, which means that nobody vests himself on his own authority. Then each garment gets its prayer, and every prayer is a verse of Scripture. Over the sticharion, Isaiah 61:10, "he hath put on me a robe of salvation, and with a garment of gladness hath he clothed me". Over the epitrachelion, the oil running down the beard of Aaron to the hem of his clothing (Psalm 132:2 in the Septuagint numbering, 133:2 in the Hebrew). Over the belt, "Blessed is God, who girdeth me about with power" (Psalm 17:32). Over the right cuff, Exodus 15:6, the right hand of God that shattered the enemies, and over the left, Psalm 118:73, "Thy hands have made me, and fashioned me". Over the epigonation, Psalm 44:3, spoken to the King: "Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Powerful One". Over the phelonion, Psalm 131:9, "Thy Priests, O Lord, shall put on righteousness". Then he washes his hands with Psalm 25 before touching anything. Read the sequence as a whole and one feature stands out. In almost every one of them the actor is God and the man is the object. He is clothed, poured upon, girded, made and fashioned. Not one of them says that he is worthy of any of it.
The deacon's wings and the bishop's sheep

The deacon wears the sticharion and the orarion, the long band on his left shoulder that he raises with two fingers at every petition and binds crosswise about himself before communion. The received reading is that it is a wing. The oldest Byzantine commentators say so without hedging. Germanus of Constantinople, in the eighth century, describes the presbyters covered by their stoles the way the seraphim are covered by wings, and the deacons moving about in the thin linen wings of their oraria as ministering spirits sent out for service. Many oraria carry the angelic hymn embroidered on them. The priest's epitrachelion is the same band brought round the neck and doubled, and without it no sacrament is served. Germanus reads it as the cloth by which Christ was led away bound to his Passion, so that the priest wears the bond of the one he stands for. Symeon of Thessalonica, seven centuries later, gives it two senses at once: the enlightening grace that comes down from the Father of lights, and the yoke of Christ under which the priest may do nothing of his own. The bishop wears a sakkos in place of the phelonion, and over it the omophorion, and this one the Church never left vague. It was made of wool rather than linen because it is the sheep. When it is laid on his shoulders at his consecration the people cry Axios, and at that moment rather than earlier, because by then he already has everything a priest has. He is wearing the wandering nature of man on his own shoulders, the way the shepherd in Luke 15 carries it home.
Not a costume, and not a merit

Two errors sit on either side of this. The first says that finery at the altar is worldliness. Jerome answered it directly, replying to a man who had written that the bravery of dress and ornament is an enemy of God. What enmity is there, Jerome asks, if my tunic is cleaner than usual, or if the bishop, priest or deacon walks in white at the offering of the sacrifices? On that reasoning the clergy, the monks, the widows and the virgins are all in spiritual danger unless the people can see them begrimed with dirt and clad in rags. Mistaking squalor for humility is not humility. The second error is the opposite one, and Chrysostom names it from the pulpit at Antioch: honour the body of Christ, and do not honour him with silken garments here while he perishes of cold outside. He takes care not to be misread. He is not forbidding generosity toward the church, he is saying that the works of mercy belong with it, and before it. The vestment is a sign, and a sign becomes a lie when the man wearing it will not feed the person it points at.

None of this begins with the clergy. Cyril of Jerusalem told the newly baptized that when they took off their tunic at the door of the font it was an image of putting off the old man with his deeds, and that stripped and naked they were imitating Christ stripped on the Cross. Then they were clothed in white. "For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27), and the parable of the wedding feast warns that a man can sit at the table without the garment. So the next time you are standing in a service and do not understand what you are seeing, take it this way. The man at the altar is wearing, in a form you can look at, what was given to you at your own baptism, and every prayer he said while putting it on was a request that his own person be got out of the way. Watch the deacon lift the orarion at "Let us pray to the Lord". Watch the bishop's shoulders. That is the sheep.

florilegium.author: St Gregory the Theologian
florilegium.work: Oration 2, In Defence of His Flight to Pontus
florilegium.text: I hear from Moses himself, when God spoke to him, that, although many were bidden to come to the mount, one of whom was even Aaron, with his two sons who were priests, and seventy elders of the senate, the rest were ordered to worship afar off, and Moses alone to draw near, and the people were not to go up with him. For it is not everyone who may draw near to God, but only one who, like Moses, can bear the glory of God.
florilegium.gloss: The reason there is a vesting at all. Gregory's whole argument is about who may approach and on what terms, and the garments are the visible form of that question.

florilegium.author: St Clement of Rome
florilegium.text: For his own peculiar services are assigned to the high priest, and their own proper place is prescribed to the priests, and their own special ministrations devolve on the Levites. The layman is bound by the laws that pertain to laymen.
florilegium.gloss: The earliest Christian letter outside the New Testament already reasons about the Church's ministry from the Aaronic orders. Ranked and distinguished service is not a later Byzantine overlay.

florilegium.author: St Polycrates of Ephesus
florilegium.work: Letter to Victor of Rome, preserved in Eusebius, Church History
florilegium.text: Among these are Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who fell asleep in Hierapolis; and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter, who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus; and, moreover, John, who was both a witness and a teacher, who reclined upon the bosom of the Lord, and, being a priest, wore the sacerdotal plate.
florilegium.gloss: About 190, the Bishop of Ephesus writes of the Apostle John as wearing the petalon, the golden plate of Exodus 28 engraved "Holiness of the Lord". Historians dispute whether he means it literally or as a title of honour. Either way the sentence shows how early the priesthood of Aaron was being read onto Christian ministers.

florilegium.author: The Apostolic Constitutions
florilegium.work: Book VIII, the Constitution of James the Brother of John
florilegium.text: Let the high priest, therefore, together with the priests, pray by himself; and let him put on his shining garment, and stand at the altar, and make the sign of the cross upon his forehead with his hand, and say: The grace of Almighty God, and the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost, be with you all.
florilegium.gloss: A fourth-century Syrian church order. The bishop puts on a distinct garment at a distinct moment, immediately before the anaphora, and the rubric explains nothing, because it did not need to.

florilegium.author: The Council of Laodicea
florilegium.work: Canons of the Council of Laodicea in Phrygia
florilegium.reference: Canons 22 and 23, printed here consecutively (NPNF Second Series, vol. 14)
florilegium.text: The subdeacon has no right to wear an orarium, nor to leave the doors. The readers and singers have no right to wear an orarium, and to read or sing thus [habited].
florilegium.gloss: Two canons of a fourth-century local council, naming the orarion and reserving it. A vestment is not forbidden to the lower orders unless it already marks a higher one. This is the earliest hard evidence in the East for the deacon's stole.

florilegium.author: The Council in Trullo (Quinisext)
florilegium.work: Canons of the Council in Trullo, 692
florilegium.text: None of those who are in the catalogue of the clergy shall wear clothes unsuited to them, either while still living in town or when on a journey: but they shall wear such clothes as are assigned to those who belong to the clergy. And if any one shall violate this canon, he shall be cut off for one week.
florilegium.gloss: By 692 clerical dress is a matter of discipline with a penalty attached. What a cleric wears is treated as a public statement about what he is, in the street as much as at the altar.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the sticharion; the text is Isaiah 61:10
florilegium.text: My soul shall exult in the Lord; for he hath put on me a robe of salvation, and with a garment of gladness hath he clothed me: he hath crowned me, as a bridegroom, with a crown, and adorned me, as a bride, with adornment.
florilegium.gloss: The first garment and the first sentence, and everything in it is done to the man by someone else. He is clothed, crowned, adorned. He does not claim to have prepared himself for anything.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the epitrachelion; the text is Psalm 132:2 in the Septuagint numbering (133:2 Hebrew)
florilegium.text: Blessed is God, who poureth forth his grace upon his Priests, as unguent on the head, that runneth down upon the beard, even the beard of Aaron, that runneth down upon the border of his garment.
florilegium.gloss: The vestment without which no sacrament is served, and its prayer names Aaron out loud. Grace is pictured as oil that keeps running downward, head to beard to hem, which is to say that it never stops at the man it lands on.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the zone; the text is Psalm 17:32 in the Septuagint numbering (18:32 Hebrew)
florilegium.text: Blessed is God, who girdeth me about with power, and hath made my way blameless, always: now, and ever, and unto the ages of the ages. Amen.
florilegium.gloss: A belt is a working garment, and this is a working prayer. Strength for the task, and a blameless way, in that order.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the epimanika, the first prayer over the right hand and the second over the left; the texts are Exodus 15:6 and Psalm 118:73 (119:73 Hebrew)
florilegium.text: Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength: thy right hand, O Lord, hath shattered the enemies; and in the multitude of thy glory thou hast crushed the adversaries. Thy hands have made me, and fashioned me: instruct me, and I shall learn thy commandments.
florilegium.gloss: Two prayers for two hands, and neither is about the priest's hands. The right calls on the hand of God, the left confesses that his own hands are a made thing. Later custom also reads the cuffs as the bonds on Christ's wrists.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the epigonation, worn by bishops and by honoured presbyters; the text is Psalm 44:3 in the Septuagint numbering (45:3 Hebrew)
florilegium.text: Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Powerful One, in thy bloom and thy beauty; and go forward, and proceed prosperously, and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and thy right hand shall guide thee wondrously, always: now, and ever, and unto the ages of the ages. Amen.
florilegium.gloss: The stiff diamond of brocade at the knee, traditionally read as the sword of the Spirit which is the word of God. Note who is being addressed. The psalm speaks to the King, not to the man putting the vestment on. He is not being armed, he is standing beside the one who is.

florilegium.author: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: The prayers of the vesting, in the Greek and English edition of J. N. W. B. Robertson (London, 1894), pp. 199-203
florilegium.reference: At the phelonion; the text is Psalm 131:9 in the Septuagint numbering (132:9 Hebrew)
florilegium.text: Thy Priests, O Lord, shall put on righteousness, and thy Pure Ones shall exult with exultation, always: now, and ever, and unto the ages of the ages. Amen.
florilegium.gloss: The outermost garment, the one the congregation actually sees, and its prayer is in the plural and in the future. Not "I am righteous" but "thy priests shall put on righteousness".

florilegium.author: Isabel Florence Hapgood
florilegium.work: Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church, The Symbolism of the Church
florilegium.text: But the Deacon binds his Stole about him in the form of a cross shortly before the Holy Gifts are consecrated, thus typifying the wings of the Angels who serve about the Altar, as the Deacons themselves typify the Cherubim and Seraphim. Sometimes the Angelic song, "Holy, Holy, Holy," is embroidered upon the Stole.
florilegium.gloss: Hapgood is a translator and compiler, not a Father, but her 1906 service book is the standard English one and it records the received explanation faithfully. The angelic reading of the orarion is the oldest one attached to it.

florilegium.author: St Jerome of Stridon
florilegium.text: What enmity, I should like to know, is there towards God if my tunic is cleaner than usual, or if the bishop, priest, or deacon, or any other ecclesiastics, at the offering of the sacrifices walk in white? Beware, you clergy; beware, you monks; widows and virgins, you are in peril unless the people see you begrimed with dirt, and clad in rags.
florilegium.gloss: Jerome is answering a man who had written that the bravery of dress and ornament is an enemy of God. His reply is that on such a rule every clean-living Christian stands condemned. The Church keeps a set of clothes for the offering because the offering is not the same thing as the rest of life.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.work: Homilies on the Gospel of St Matthew
florilegium.text: Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here you honor Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness. For He that said, This is my body, and by His word confirmed the fact, This same said, You saw me an hungered, and fed me not; and, Inasmuch as you did it not to one of the least of these, you did it not to me.
florilegium.gloss: The necessary correction, and it comes from the Father whose Liturgy carries the vesting prayers. In the next paragraph he guards the other side too, saying he does not forbid generosity toward the church but requires the works of mercy alongside it, and before it.

florilegium.author: St Cyril of Jerusalem
florilegium.text: As soon, then, as you entered, you put off your tunic; and this was an image of putting off the old man with his deeds. Having stripped yourselves, you were naked; in this also imitating Christ, who was stripped naked on the Cross, and by His nakedness put off from Himself the principalities and powers, and openly triumphed over them on the tree.
florilegium.gloss: Before any clergyman is vested, every Christian is stripped and reclothed. The logic of vesting is the baptismal logic, and it belongs to the laity first.

scripture.note: Holy apparel for Aaron, for honour and glory, with the garments named one by one. The command is God's, not a human sense of occasion.
Beseleel filled with a divine spirit of wisdom and understanding for the work. The craft that makes the vestments is itself called a gift of the Spirit.
The plate of pure gold on the mitre, engraved "Holiness of the Lord". This is the petalon Polycrates says the Apostle John wore.
Linen inside the inner court, and the robes laid up in the chambers of the sanctuary before the priests go out to the people. The garments belong to the service, not to the man.
The prayer said over the sticharion. The robe of salvation and the garment of joy, put on the wearer by someone else.
The prayer at the epitrachelion (133:2 in the Hebrew numbering). Oil running from the head down the beard of Aaron to the hem.
The prayer at the belt (18:32 in the Hebrew numbering). It is God who girds with strength and makes the way blameless.
The prayer over the right cuff. The prayer over the left is Psalm 118:73 (119:73 Hebrew), "Thy hands have made me, and fashioned me".
The prayer at the epigonation (45:3 in the Hebrew numbering). The sword is girded on the King, not on the priest.
The prayer at the phelonion (132:9 in the Hebrew numbering). Thy priests shall clothe themselves with righteousness, future and plural.
The shepherd lays the found sheep on his shoulders. The omophorion is that sheep, which is why it was made of wool.
As many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. Every Christian is vested; the clergy wear a visible form of it.
Christ himself seen clothed to the foot and girt with a golden girdle. The pattern the sanctuary imitates is not on earth.
